ready1_open_rewrite.rewritten_question_text: The figure below is a flood frequency curve calculated by a certain watershed management unit from long-term hydrological data (1875—1975). If it is calculated using hydrological data from more recent years (1945—1975), then there is a phenomenon of increased flood frequency. Please answer the following questions accordingly. <image1> The original once-in-a-hundred-years flood level, on the flood frequency curve for 1945—1975, has a recurrence interval of approximately how many years?

ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure, the vertical axis is labeled “water level (meters),” and the horizontal axis is labeled “recurrence interval,” with scale marks including 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 20, 50, 100, etc. There are two flood frequency curves in the figure, labeled respectively “1875—1975” and “1945—1975.” The curve on the left corresponds to the more recent years 1945—1975, and the curve on the right corresponds to the longer period 1875—1975. A horizontal dashed line is also drawn on the figure, labeled “water level at which disasters begin to appear,” but this question mainly reads the corresponding relationship of the once-in-a-hundred-years flood level between the two curves. Then reason: The “original once-in-a-hundred-years flood level” in the question refers to the water level corresponding to a recurrence interval of 100 years on the 1875—1975 curve. Move horizontally along that water level to the 1945—1975 curve, then read the horizontal axis downward from the intersection point; its recurrence interval can be read as approximately 50 years. Therefore, the original once-in-a-hundred-years flood level, on the flood frequency curve for 1945—1975, has a recurrence interval of about 50 years.
